title: What changes the maintenance plan?
subtitle: One people-powered approach, three explicit assumptions.
summary: The team used a reproducible model to ask which practical assumption changes a maintenance plan. It compares ways of providing power, package access and human confirmation to parked C-arms. The figures below hold the people-powered approach constant and vary the modeled scenario.
metric_label: Modeled share of the 12-device fleet patched by day 14

rows.model_change: 120-minute installation; modeled package availability on half of devices

rows.exact_source_scenario_label: Install shrinks to 30 min (A/B slots, vendor side)
rows.model_change: Installation duration changed from 120 to 30 minutes; other base parameters retained

rows.exact_source_scenario_label: Every C-arm gets the package while in use (network in every OR)
rows.model_change: All devices receive the update package while in use; installation duration remains 120 minutes

interpretation: Within this model, making the update package available during use changes the people-powered result much more than shortening installation alone. This identifies connectivity as a question to validate; it does not establish a real-world clinical benefit.

methodology.design: Seeded stochastic simulation with common random numbers: each architecture receives the same generated hospital, procedures, emergencies, alarms and modeled human responses within a run.
methodology.implementation: Pure JavaScript model used in Node and browser. Reuses team window-planning rules and scorer; architecture alternatives change how power, data, switch-on and physical assistance reach the device.
methodology.metric_definition: For each run, count devices with patchedDay <= deadline - 1, divide by fleet size, then take the arithmetic mean across runs. Display percentages are rounded to whole numbers exactly as the source report does.
methodology.distribution_note: Stored P10–P90 values describe the distribution across simulated runs, not confidence intervals or clinical uncertainty. A mean can fall below P10 if a small number of runs perform much worse.
methodology.verification_performed: Read original RESULTS.md, generated results.json, model.js, run.cjs and source-provenance record. Reader values are selected directly from result fields and match the source table after rounding. The simulation was not rerun or calibrated in this review.

limitations: All hospitals, patients/procedures, devices, people and outcomes are synthetic. No measured hospital data underlies these figures.
Almost all model inputs are explicit assumptions. Interview estimates labeled Siemens in comments are still not independent measured validation.
Human acceptance, moving/parking behavior, network availability, emergency demand and physical success are parameterized guesses; changing them can change the ranking.
The source uses 200 base runs and 100 runs for each changed scenario. These are sensitivity illustrations, not controlled trials or a proof of causal effectiveness.

The source itself states: “These are not forecasts, and they don’t belong on a pitch slide.” Present results inside the engineering reader with model context, never as portfolio impact or product-performance claims.
One synthetic high-demand device frequently fails to obtain an acceptable window. The model does not show that every device can be safely updated.
No hospital integration, authenticated approval, physical robot action or real update was executed. Implementation and clinical validation remain future work.
Do not include cost-benefit or cost-saving claims; the source’s cost figures are rough assumptions and are omitted from this compact reader.

display_requirements.caption: Source simulation, not measured hospital outcomes. Same people-powered approach; the scenario assumption changes.
